title: Serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling, benchmarking and runbooks
author: Ava Chen
body:
Summary:
This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling design, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite, release notes summary, known issues, and operational runbooks used by the Serving Runtime team. It is intended as the canonical reference for engineers and oncall responders working on request path performance, scheduling, and GPU/kernels optimization.

1. Introduction and scope
- Audience: serving runtime engineers, SREs, perf engineers, and platform owners.
- Scope: architecture overview, kernel scheduling policy, profiling methodology, benchmark definitions, runbooks for common incidents, and pointers to team wiki pages.

2. Architecture overview
Short intro: The serving runtime is a modular, high-throughput inference engine designed for multi-tenant, latency-sensitive LLM workloads. Design goals are predictability (p99 latency SLAs), throughput efficiency, and graceful degradation.

Key components:
- Frontend API gateway (route-level routing, authentication, quota enforcement).
- Dispatcher (request aggregation, batching controller, routing policy).
- Scheduler (per-GPU kernel scheduler, occupancy manager, kernel selection cache).
- Worker (model execution, KV cache management, token generation loops).
- Telemetry and control plane (tracing, metrics, rollout configuration, feature flags).

Design notes:
- Continuous batching is implemented in the dispatcher with adaptive batching windows tuned per-route.
- KV cache is sharded per-model-variant and pinned to GPU memory to avoid PCIe fetches during hot prefixes.
- Kernel selection uses a precompiled manifest (JSON) mapping model-ops -> candidate kernels prioritized by hardware and sequence-length.

3. Kernel scheduling design
Overview:
The scheduler balances three axes: latency SLOs (minimize p99), throughput (maximize tokens/sec), and fairness (isolate noisy tenants).

Scheduling primitives and policies:
- Preemptive time-slices: long-running kernels (e.g., large matmuls for wide models) are allowed preemptive slices with checkpointing to KV cache when possible.
- Priority classes: real-time (p99 SLA <= 300ms), interactive (p99 <= 1s), background (batch jobs, no latency SLO).
- Tenant weight buckets: each tenant is assigned a weight that affects scheduling share; weights configured via Dedicated reservations or runtime policy.
- Kernel co-location rules: small kernels (sequence < 128) are co-located using CUDA stream isolation when memory headroom permits; large kernels get exclusive streams.

Kernel selection flow (simplified):
1) Dispatcher provides model_id, sequence_length, batch_size, and target_slo.
2) Scheduler looks up the manifest for candidate kernels and filters by device capability and memory headroom.
3) Cost model scores candidates (latency estimate, peak memory, flop utilization).
4) Scheduler selects kernel and assigns to a GPU lane with expected start time.

Operational knobs:
- SLO headroom threshold: default 20% (i.e., maintain 20% free compute margin for bursty requests).
- Co-location memory floor: 10% of GPU free memory must remain to allow safe co-location.
- Preemption quantum: 16ms by default (tunable per model-family).

4. Profiling playbook (how to collect and triage perf regressions)
Purpose: give a reproducible method to profile regressions and attribute root causes to kernel choices, batching changes, or infra variations.

When to run profiling:
- p99 or p95 increase > 15% for a route for three consecutive hours
- Increase in GPU OOM events or kernel launch failures
- Perf regressions flagged by CI benchmark guardrails

Steps:
1) Gather baseline: collect historical run metrics for the route (last 72h): p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, batching window distribution, effective batch sizes.
2) Reproduce in isolated staging: pin the same model version, model config, and input prompt set; run synthetic replay at production QPS using ./tools/replay --route=<route> --qps=<qps> --seed=stable.
3) Capture traces: enable full tracing for the replay and collect: dispatcher timing, scheduler decisions, kernel manifests, CUDA profiler output (nvprof or Nsight), and GPU sm_util/mem_util metrics.
4) Annotate traces: map kernel launches to manifest entries and measure kernel time distribution, queueing delays, and preemption events.
5) Compare kernels: run microbenchmarks for competing kernels with same shape (sequence, batch) using ./tools/kernel-bench --kernel=<name> --shapes='[128,1]'.
6) Action: depending on root cause: update kernel manifest weights, adjust preemption quantum, tune batching window, or revert recent rollout.

Profiling tips and commands:
- Recommended capture sequence:
  - tracerctl start --level=debug --routes=<route>
  - ./tools/replay --route=<route> --qps=50 --duration=300
  - nvprof --profile-from-start off --log-file /tmp/nvprof.out ./bin/worker --profile
- Use the perf dashboard at /dashboards/serving-runtime/profiling to visualize kernel timelines and preemption events.

5. Benchmarking suite
Purpose: standardize performance baselines for model variants and hardware configurations. Benchmarks are automated in CI and run monthly across representative models and prompt sets.

Benchmark categories:
- Latency microbenchmarks: single-request p50/p95/p99 across shapes (seq: 16,64,128,512) and batch sizes (1..8).
- Throughput benchmarks: steady-state tokens/sec at target p95 constraints.
- Cost-efficiency: effective tokens/sec per GPU-hour and tokens-per-dollar estimates.
- Cold-start and warm-cache: evaluate cold KV-cache startup and steady-state cached paths.

Benchmark harness and artifacts:
- repo: infra/benchmarks/serving-runtime
- harness: bench_runner.py which orchestrates model loads, synthetic replay, and collects metrics to bench-output/<run-id>.json
- baselines stored in bench-baselines/<model-family>/<hardware-profile>.json

Example benchmark config (JSON):
{
  "model": "rwkv-3b-quantized-4bit",
  "hardware": "A100-80GB",
  "shapes": [16,64,128,512],
  "batch_sizes": [1,2,4,8],
  "warmup_seconds": 60,
  "duration_seconds": 600
}

Acceptance criteria for new kernel or quantization profile:
- p95 cannot regress more than 10% vs baseline for same hardware and model-family
- tokens/sec per GPU must be >= baseline * 0.95
- memory footprint must be <= baseline + 5%

6. Release notes (summary for last major runtime release)
Release: 2028-05 Major runtime 4.2.0
Highlights:
- Kernel manifest rewrite to support dynamic kernel sharding and improved flop utilization (+12% tokens/sec for long sequences).
- Preemptive scheduling support introduced with 16ms quantum (experimental flagged).
- New profiling dashboard integrated with tracing and kernel-level heatmaps.
- Default batching window algorithm improved to reduce latency tail on interactive routes.

Notable fixes:
- Fixed a memory leak in KV cache eviction logic causing elevated OOMs under high prefix diversity.
- Corrected a regression in co-location guard that caused unnecessary exclusive kernel placements.

Upgrade notes:
- Rolling upgrade recommended (canary 5% -> 25% -> 100%) with monitoring of p95 and OOM rate.
- If customer uses pinned model variants, confirm kernel manifest compatibility or pin to previous runtime until manifest migration is scheduled.

7. Known issues (operationally relevant)
- Issue #2028-14: Intermittent p99 spikes on routes with highly variable sequence lengths (>50% variance). Workaround: set max_sequence_bucket per-route or enforce sequence normalization at dispatcher.
- Issue #2028-21: Rare kernel launch failures on mixed GPU fleets when CUDA driver mismatch present. Workaround: ensure driver version 535.54+ on all pool nodes; fallback to software kernels via feature flag runtime.disable_gpu_fastpath=true.
- Issue #2028-30: KV cache warmup causes initial cold-start latency for multi-prefix loads. Mitigation: prewarm heavy prefixes via prefetcher --route=<route> --prefix-list=heavy_prefixes.txt.

8. Runtime runbooks (quick operational playbooks)
Runbook: High p99 on interactive route- Severity: Sev2- Owner: serving-runtime-oncall
Steps:
1) Check route dashboard: p50/p95/p99, batch size distribution, effective QPS.
2) Check GPU metrics: sm_util, mem_util, queue_length, OOM events.
3) Run quick trace capture for 5 minutes: tracerctl capture --route=<route> --out=/tmp/trace.json
4) If preemption events are frequent and queueing > 20ms, temporarily increase preemption quantum to 32ms: schedulerctl set preemption-quantum=32 --route=<route>
5) If OOMs observed, enable route fallback to smaller model-variant: routesctl set-fallback --route=<route> --model=<small-variant>
6) If root cause is rollout, rollback to prior runtime using canary manager: rolloutctl rollback --id=<canary-id>
7) Create incident and assign to perf lead; attach traces and bench outputs.

Runbook: GPU OOM on node- Severity: Sev1- Owner: infra-gpu-pool
Steps:
1) Mark node as unschedulable: k8s cordon <node-id>
2) Inspect dmesg and kernel logs for OOM killer traces and driver errors.
3) Collect worker logs: journalctl -u worker -o short-iso > /tmp/worker.log
4) If OOM is caused by recent model rollout, revert model or evict large KV shards: kvctl evict --model=<model> --shard=<shard-id>
5) Replace node if hardware error; otherwise restart driver and node services, then uncordon.

Appendix A: Example kernel manifest snippet (JSON)
{
  "model_family": "rwkv-3b",
  "kernels": [
    {"name": "matmul_opt_v2", "seq_min": 1, "seq_max": 128, "expected_latency_ms": 2.4, "memory_bytes": 1200000000},
    {"name": "matmul_shard_v1", "seq_min": 129, "seq_max": 2048, "expected_latency_ms": 18.2, "memory_bytes": 4200000000}
  ]
}

Appendix B: Useful CLI tools
- ./tools/replay -- replay production-like requests to staging
- ./tools/kernel-bench -- microbench kernels with exact shapes
- tracerctl -- control tracing and capture traces
- schedulerctl -- runtime scheduling configuration
- kvctl -- manage KV cache shards

Appendix C: Configuration table (defaults)
- p99_slo_default: "300ms"
- slo_headroom_fraction: "0.20"
- preemption_quantum_ms: "16"
- co_location_memory_floor_fraction: "0.10"
- default_batching_window_ms: "12"
